primitives.name: Product Space Ring Closure
primitives.verbatim_quote: If S and T are rings of subsets of X and Y respectively, then the class R of all finite, disjoint unions of rectangles of the form A× B, where A ε S and B ε T, is a ring.
primitives.latex: \text{Let } \mathcal{R} = \{\cup_{i=1}^n (A_i \times B_i) : A_i \in \mathcal{S}, B_i \in \mathcal{T}\}, \text{ then } \mathcal{R} \text{ is a ring.}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'S': 'ring of subsets of X, dimensionless', 'T': 'ring of subsets of Y, dimensionless', 'A': 'subset of X, dimensionless', 'B': 'subset of Y, dimensionless', 'R': 'class of finite disjoint unions of rectangles, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: S and T are rings; A ⊆ X, B ⊆ Y; finite disjoint unions exist.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When S or T fails to be a ring or when unions are not disjoint.

layer2.mapping: The ring structure of R mirrors the algebraic closure properties of S and T under intersection and difference operations.
layer2.telemetry: Verification of closure under finite intersections and differences of rectangles.

primitives.name: Rectangle Intersection Property
primitives.verbatim_quote: We observe first that the intersection of two sets of the form A × B is another set of that form.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'A_1, A_2': 'subsets of X, dimensionless', 'B_1, B_2': 'subsets of Y, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: A₁, A₂ ⊆ X; B₁, B₂ ⊆ Y; intersection exists.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When A₁ ∩ A₂ or B₁ ∩ B₂ is empty, intersection trivializes.

layer2.mapping: Intersection property enables recursive decomposition of product sets into simpler components.
layer2.telemetry: Validation of distributive behavior of Cartesian products under set intersection.

primitives.name: Disjoint Union Decomposition
primitives.verbatim_quote: If, for instance, 4 is the disjoint union of A1 and A2 and B = B1 = B2, then A ⊃ A1, A ⊃ A2, B ⊃ B1, B ⊃ B2, so that E ⊃ E1 ∪ E2.
primitives.latex: E = E_1 \cup E_2 \text{ where } E_i = A_i \times B \text{ and } A = A_1 \cup A_2 \text{ disjoint}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'A': 'union of A1 and A2, dimensionless', 'B': 'common subset of Y, dimensionless', 'E': 'product set, dimensionless', 'E1, E2': 'disjoint components of E, dimensionless'}
primitives.breakdown_regime: When A1 and A2 overlap or B1 ≠ B2.

layer2.mapping: Decomposition preserves topological and measure-theoretic properties of product spaces.
layer2.telemetry: Consistency check of component-wise disjointness in product space partitioning.

The derivation begins with defining a ring of subsets S on X and T on Y. From these, we construct the class R of finite disjoint unions of rectangles A × B where A ∈ S and B ∈ T. To prove R is a ring, we verify closure under finite intersections and differences. For intersections, (A₁ × B₁) ∩ (A₂ × B₂) = (A₁ ∩ A₂) × (B₁ ∩ B₂), which remains in R due to S and T being rings. Differences are handled by expressing them as disjoint unions of rectangles, maintaining closure. This ensures R inherits the ring structure from S and T. Dualities arise in how disjointness interacts with projections onto factors. Failure modes occur when S or T do not close under intersection or difference, or when unions are not properly disjoint.
